transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah… I came in because I’m just not sleeping right anymore. Like, barely at all some nights. I’ll get in bed and I’m exhausted, but then I’m just lying there, staring at the ceiling, and if I hear rain or even start thinking about that bluff giving way, my head just won’t shut off. It’s like I’m back there in my mind and I can’t settle down.

And then when I finally do pass out, it’s not like real sleep. I’ll wake up sweating from dreams, all tense, and it feels like I was fighting all night instead of resting. Then I’ve got to go into the call center and put on the voice and talk to people like I’m fine, but I feel like I never slept at all. It’s been wearing me down.
Can you tell me more about that bluff incident? Were you involved in an accident or a traumatic event recently?

I mean… I don’t really know how to explain it cleanly. I keep calling it “the bluff incident” because that’s what my head grabs onto, but I’m not sure I can give you, like, a neat accident report or anything. It wasn’t like I sat down and wrote out what happened, and honestly when you ask it straight like that I kind of freeze up.

What I can say is it had to do with that bluff giving way, or at least that’s the part that sticks. That image, that feeling of the ground not being safe, like something solid suddenly isn’t solid… that’s what keeps coming up for me. But I don’t know if I’m answering your question right, because I don’t really have the words for whether to call it an accident or a traumatic event. It just felt bad enough that my brain keeps going back there.
When you say your brain keeps going back to that moment at the bluff, do you find yourself having sudden, vivid memories of it — like it's happening all over again?

Yeah… yeah, that does happen. Not all the time in a predictable way, but it’ll just hit me out of nowhere. Like I’ll be sitting at my desk with the headset on, trying to listen to somebody talk about their bill or whatever, and suddenly I’m not really there for a second.

It’s like I hear rocks sliding, even if there’s nothing making that sound. Or I get this flash of my leg being stuck under me, and my body reacts before I can think. For a minute it feels like I’m back on that trail, not in the office. I know I’m technically at work, I know there’s a computer in front of me, but it’s like my brain pulls me back there so fast that it takes me a second to catch up.

And it’s not like I sit there trying to remember it. That’s the part that messes with me. It just pops into my head. I could be doing something normal, and then suddenly I’m right back in that feeling.
Have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of that experience at the bluff?

Yeah… I have. More than I want to admit, honestly.

I don’t go near the coast trails now. Like, before, that was kind of a normal thing for me and my friends — we’d go hiking, mess around, take pictures, whatever. And now if someone even mentions that area, or anything close to the bluff, my whole body just kind of locks up. I’ll make excuses like I’m working or I’m tired or I don’t have a ride, but really I just… I can’t make myself go out there.

And I’ve been dodging my hiking buddies too, which makes me feel bad because they didn’t do anything wrong. They’ll text like, “Hey, you trying to go out this weekend?” or send a picture of some trail, and I’ll just leave it sitting there. Sometimes I’ll type something and delete it, because even talking about going back out there makes my chest tighten. It’s like if I answer, then I’m letting that whole thing come closer again, so I just avoid the conversation completely.
